catalog_quote: Crow words have a lexical accent which may occur on any vowel of the stem. Within a long vowel or diphthong, the lexical accent may occur on either mora. The pitch pattern of the word is derived by the following rule (cf. Old Horn (1974). (28) High Pitch Plateau Rule: Within a word, create a high pitch plateau extending from the first mora of the leftmost long vowel or diphthong rightward to the marked lexical accent; all other syllables have low pitch. If lexical accent occurs on the first mora of a long vowel or diphthong, the syllable has falling tone. If lexical accent occurs on the second mora, the syllable will have level high or slightly rising tone (Matthews, 1981). The following examples are minimal or near-minimal pairs demonstrating the lexicality of accent. ... (29) Lexicality of accent: a. sheék 'he/she said it' b. shéek 'he/she died' c. balé 'wood' d. bále 'money'. ... Whe…
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Crow is not in the catalog. this search of works with stress in the title had one title item, Gordon 1972 'Pitch Accent in Crow' (IJAL 38:191-200, doi:10.1086/465205): relevant (dedicated account of Crow word-level pitch accent, one of four classic accounts per Ko 2023 fn.4) but closed everywhere checked (OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar closed, no repository copy, archive.org 0 hits, HathiTrust has no IJAL v.38 and in-copyright volumes are search-only, publisher page 403) -- priority high to acquire via library. The best first-hand statement actually read is Wallace 1993 (UCLA diss., open PDF already held by the project, scanned) sec. 2.6 p. 23: Crow has a lexical accent that may fall on any vowel of the stem and on either mora of a long vowel, with minimal pairs, plus a High Pitch Plateau Rule deriving the surface contour and an Accent Conflict Rule for complex words; i.e. lexical/unpredictable pitch accent. Supporting notes from Ko 2023 (accent tends to fall on the verbal stem; shifts with 2nd-person prefixes) and Lowie 1941 p. 22 (2nd person throws accent toward the word beginning). Graczyk 2007 pp. 19-23 remains the best modern description but is print-only (Google Books no preview).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Crow is a lexical pitch accent language: each stem carries one accent whose position is unpredictable (any vowel, either mora of a long vowel/diphthong; minimal pairs like sheék 'said' vs shéek 'died', balé 'wood' vs bale 'money'). Surface pitch is derived: high plateau from the leftmost long vowel/diphthong up to the accented mora, low elsewhere (all post-accent syllables low). One accent per phonological word; in compounds/incorporation/suffixation the Accent Conflict Rule deletes the first accent if it is morph-final, otherwise deletes the second.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; the High Pitch Plateau (high pitch on pre-accent long vowels and intervening syllables) is a tonal spread, not a secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Sec. 2.7.4 'maverick suffixes with lexical accent' and 2.8 evidential suffixes that keep their own accent; 2.9.1 stem vowel shortening with accent shift in agreement forms (second-person prefix shifts accent, also noted by Lowie 1941 p.22 and Ko 2023 p.81).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain of the High Pitch Plateau Rule and the one-accent constraint is the phonological word (used as a wordhood diagnostic); examples are citation/declarative word forms.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Crow proper (crow1244, ISO cro), Crow Agency / Lodge Grass, Montana speakers; Wallace's consultants were from Crow Agency area (1987-1992 fieldwork). No dialect split is at issue.

new_statements.citation: Wallace, Karen Kay. 1993. Verb Incorporation and Agreement in Crow. PhD dissertation, UCLA. Section 2.6 'The pitch accent system', p. 23.
new_statements.locator: sec. 2.6, printed p. 23 (PDF page 36); rule (28) and examples (29)-(31) pp. 23-24
new_statements.reading: Crow has lexically specified (unpredictable) pitch accent: the accent can fall on any vowel of the stem, and even on either mora of a long vowel or diphthong, with minimal pairs such as sheek 'he said it' vs sheek 'he died' (accent on different moras) and bale 'wood' vs bale 'money' (p. 24, ex. 29). The surface pitch contour is then derived by a high-pitch plateau from the first long vowel up to the accented mora. In complex words only one accent survives, by an Accent Conflict Rule (sec. 2.7, p. 24): the first morph's accent deletes if it is on that morph's final vowel, otherwise the second morph's accent deletes. For a catalog's classification this is a lexical/unpredictable pitch accent language (not fixed or weight-based stress). Ko 2023 (p. 129 area, line 3667) adds only that accent 'tends to fall on the verbal stem' and shifts with second-person prefixes; Lowie 1941 (p. 22) notes the second person 'tends to throw the accent toward the beginning of the word'. Graczyk 2007 pp. 19-23 (cited by Ko as the general description) and Gordon 1972 were not obtainable.

new_statements.quote: Verbs with this prefix form a distinct conjugation. The shift in accent in the first and second persons is noteworthy. The verb in the text is conjugated as follows: burutsi'ky, diru'tsiky, du'tsiky; burutu''k, diru'tu'k, du'tu'k. [p. 166] ... At one time I thought a mere difference in tone distinguished the words for fire (falling) and water (rising). I am now convinced that this was accidental and that the final vowel is lower, more open, for "fire," higher for "water." [p. 171]

Printed p. 171 (PDF p. 21), under the entry i'wira'.u-o"sau: 'At one time I thought a mere difference in tone distinguished the words for fire (falling) and wat…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing statements (Wallace 1993 lexical pitch accent that may fall on any stem vowel; Lowie 1941 p. 22 and Ko 2023 on accent shifting with person prefixes). Lowie 1930 adds an early first-hand observation of the same person-conditioned accent shift in du- verbs (burutsi'ky / diru'tsiky / du'tsiky) and a retraction of a fire/water tone contrast, so it supports 'accent is lexically/morphologically placed, not fixed' but gives no placement rule and does not say whether the accent is pitch or stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The work is a single analyzed text with word-by-word notes and has no phonology or accent section. Its symbols list (p. 157) explains vowels, consonants, aspiration and glottal stop but not the acute accent mark that Lowie writes on nearly every word. The only accent statement is incidental: in the du- (instrumental 'by hand') verb conjugation the accent moves between persons (burutsi'ky 'I' / diru'tsiky 'you' vs du'tsiky 'he'), i.e. accent position is morphologically conditioned and not fixed to one syllable; the transcribed forms show accent on various syllables (du'tsiky initial, burutsi'ky penult, bici' final, dapi'a penult). Separately Lowie retracts an earlier impression of a tone contrast between 'fire' and 'water' and attributes the difference to vowel quality. No placement rule is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: none stated; the du- verb conjugation is presented as 'noteworthy' for its accent shift in 1st/2nd person
new_statements.identity_note: Lowie 1930 describes the Crow of eastern Montana (Crow Reservation), same variety as the other sources; no dialect named.
